entries.meaning: The whole physical structure of a person or animal. ---
examples: Yoga taught me how my body actually works.
Cold water is a shock to the body.
Their bodies were still sore from Saturday's game.

entries.meaning: The limb that runs from the shoulder down to the hand. ---
examples: He broke his arm falling off a ladder.
She carried the groceries in both arms.
Put your arm around her for the photo.
entries.contrast: Russian рука covers the whole limb; English splits it — the arm ends at the wrist, and the hand takes over from there.

entries.meaning: One of the two limbs a person stands and walks on. ---
examples: My legs were killing me after the hike.
He crossed his legs and leaned back.
She hurt her left leg playing soccer.
entries.contrast: Russian нога covers the whole limb; the English leg stops at the ankle, and below that it is the foot.

entries.meaning: The part of the body below the wrist, with fingers and a thumb. ---
examples: Wash your hands before dinner.
He shook my hand and introduced himself.
Her hands were freezing without gloves.
entries.contrast: Never use hand for the whole рука — you hold a bag in your hand but carry a child in your arms.

entries.meaning: One of the four long jointed parts of the hand, not counting the thumb. ---
examples: I cut my finger chopping onions.
She ran a finger down the map.
His fingers were stained with ink.
entries.contrast: English counts the thumb separately, so a hand has four fingers plus a thumb; and a палец on the foot is a toe, never a finger.

entries.meaning: The short thick digit set apart from the other four on the hand. ---
examples: He hit his thumb with the hammer.
She scrolled through the photos with her thumb.
Both thumbs were sore from texting all day.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: THUM, one syllable.

entries.meaning: One of the five digits at the end of the foot. ---
examples: I stubbed my toe on the coffee table.
Sand got in between my toes.
He can touch his toes without bending his knees.

entries.meaning: The joint in the middle of the leg where it bends. ---
examples: My knee still hurts from the fall.
He got down on one knee to propose.
She scraped both knees on the pavement.
entries.contrast: The k is silent: NEE. Same silent k in knuckle and knife.

entries.meaning: The joint in the middle of the arm where it bends. ---
examples: He rested his elbows on the table.
I banged my elbow on the door frame.
She nudged me with her elbow.

entries.meaning: The joint where the arm meets the body. ---
examples: He carried the bag on one shoulder.
My shoulders get tight after a day at the desk.
She tapped him on the shoulder.

entries.meaning: The joint between the hand and the arm. ---
examples: She wears her watch on her left wrist.
I sprained my wrist playing tennis.
The bracelet hung loose around his wrist.
entries.contrast: The w is silent: RIST. Same silent w in wrinkle and write.

entries.meaning: The joint between the foot and the leg. ---
examples: He twisted his ankle on the trail.
The water was up to our ankles.
She has a tattoo just above her ankle.

entries.meaning: The joint on either side of the body where the leg meets the trunk. ---
examples: She broke her hip in the fall.
He stood there with his hands on his hips.
The baby rode on her hip all afternoon.

entries.meaning: The narrow part of the body between the ribs and the hips. ---
examples: These jeans are too tight in the waist.
He put an arm around her waist.
The water came up to my waist.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like waste.

entries.meaning: The front of the body between the neck and the stomach. ---
examples: He felt a sharp pain in his chest.
The kid crossed his arms over his chest.
I have a cold and it went straight to my chest.

entries.meaning: The rear surface of the body from the shoulders to the hips. ---
examples: My back has been sore all week.
He lay on his back and stared at the ceiling.
Lift with your legs, not your back.

entries.meaning: The organ that digests food, or the front of the body below the chest. ---
examples: Don't take these pills on an empty stomach.
My stomach growled through the whole meeting.
He sleeps on his stomach.
entries.contrast: The ch is a plain k sound: STUH-muk, never stow-match.

entries.meaning: The soft front part of the body below the chest, in casual speech. ---
examples: The dog rolled over for a belly rub.
He laughed until his belly hurt.
She felt the baby kick in her belly.

entries.meaning: The part of the body joining the head to the shoulders. ---
examples: I slept wrong and my neck is stiff.
She wore a thin gold chain around her neck.
The giraffe stretched its neck toward the leaves.

entries.meaning: The passage inside the neck that food and air pass through. ---
examples: I have a sore throat.
Something caught in his throat and he coughed.
Drink some tea, it will soothe your throat.

entries.meaning: The front of the head, from the forehead to the chin. ---
examples: He splashed cold water on his face.
I never forget a face.
Their faces lit up when they saw the cake.

entries.meaning: The organ you see with. ---
examples: She has her mother's eyes.
Something got in my eye.
Keep an eye on the kids by the pool.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like the pronoun I.

entries.meaning: The organ you hear with, on either side of the head. ---
examples: He whispered something in her ear.
My ears popped on the flight.
The dog perked up its ears.

entries.meaning: The part of the face you breathe and smell through. ---
examples: Her nose ran all morning.
He broke his nose in a fight.
The smell went straight up my nose.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like knows.

entries.meaning: The opening in the face used for eating and speaking. ---
examples: Don't talk with your mouth full.
He opened his mouth to argue, then stopped.
Cover your mouth when you cough.
entries.contrast: The singular ends in a voiceless th, but the plural mouths ends in a voiced th plus z: MOWTHZ.

entries.meaning: Either of the two soft edges of the mouth. ---
examples: My lips crack every winter.
She bit her lip and said nothing.
He had a cut on his upper lip.

entries.meaning: The muscular organ in the mouth used for tasting and speaking. ---
examples: I burned my tongue on the coffee.
The dog's tongue was hanging out.
Stick out your tongue and say ah.
entries.contrast: The -gue is just a single ng sound: TUNG, one syllable.

entries.meaning: The front of the jaw, below the mouth. ---
examples: He rested his chin on his hand.
She has a small scar on her chin.
Keep your chin up, it will get easier.

entries.meaning: Either side of the face below the eye. ---
examples: The baby's cheeks were bright red.
He kissed her on the cheek.
Tears ran down her cheeks.

entries.meaning: The part of the face above the eyebrows and below the hairline. ---
examples: She put a hand on his forehead to check for fever.
Sweat ran down my forehead.
He has a bruise across his forehead.
entries.contrast: Two pronunciations circulate: FOR-hed is the usual American one, while the older FOR-id still turns up.

entries.meaning: The line of hair growing above each eye. ---
examples: She raised an eyebrow but said nothing.
He has thick dark eyebrows.
She gets her eyebrows done every few weeks.

entries.meaning: One of the short hairs growing on the edge of the eyelid. ---
examples: An eyelash got in my eye.
Her eyelashes are impossibly long.
He blinked and an eyelash landed on his cheek.

entries.meaning: The fold of skin that closes over the eye. ---
examples: His eyelids were getting heavy.
She has a twitch in her left eyelid.
The doctor gently lifted my eyelid.

entries.meaning: The bone structure of the mouth that holds the teeth. ---
examples: He clenched his jaw and said nothing.
She broke her jaw in the accident.
My jaw aches from chewing gum all day.

entries.meaning: The bony frame of the head that protects the brain. ---
examples: The X-ray showed a crack in his skull.
A helmet protects your skull.
They found animal skulls in the cave.

entries.meaning: The organ inside the head that controls thought and movement. ---
examples: Your brain burns a surprising number of calories.
The scan showed no damage to his brain.
Sleep gives the brain time to sort things out.

entries.meaning: The organ that pumps blood around the body. ---
examples: My heart was pounding.
He has a heart condition.
The runner's heart rate dropped fast.
entries.contrast: Heart has the ah of car; hurt has the ur of her. Two different words.

entries.meaning: Either of the two organs in the chest used for breathing. ---
examples: He filled his lungs with cold air.
Smoking damages the lungs.
She has an infection in one lung.

entries.meaning: The large organ that cleans the blood and helps digestion. ---
examples: Too much alcohol wrecks your liver.
The tests showed his liver was fine.
The liver filters everything you drink.

entries.meaning: Either of the two organs that filter waste out of the blood. ---
examples: He donated a kidney to his brother.
Both kidneys were starting to fail.
Drink water, it is easier on your kidneys.

entries.meaning: One of the hard pieces that make up the skeleton. ---
examples: He broke a bone in his foot.
The soup is made with beef bones.
The handle is carved from bone.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: Tissue that contracts to move part of the body. ---
examples: I pulled a muscle in my back.
He has been putting on muscle since January.
Your heart is a muscle too.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: The c is silent: MUS-ul, exactly like the shellfish mussel.

entries.meaning: The outer covering of the body. ---
examples: My skin gets dry every winter.
Sunscreen protects your skin.
The lotion left my skin greasy.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: The red liquid the heart pumps through the body. ---
examples: There was blood all over the towel.
They took a sample of my blood.
The sight of blood made him dizzy.
entries.contrast: The oo sounds like the u in flood, not like food: BLUD.

entries.meaning: A fiber that carries signals between the brain and the rest of the body. ---
examples: The dentist hit a nerve.
A pinched nerve in his neck caused the pain.
The nerves in your fingertips are unusually sensitive.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Countable for the fibers; uncountable when it means courage — it takes some nerve to ask.

entries.meaning: A tube that carries blood back toward the heart. ---
examples: The nurse couldn't find a vein.
Blue veins showed through her skin.
Blood returns to the heart through the veins.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like vain and vane.

entries.meaning: A tube that carries blood away from the heart. ---
examples: Cholesterol builds up in the arteries.
The bullet missed the main artery.
An artery has thicker walls than a vein.

entries.meaning: One of the curved bones that form the cage around the chest. ---
examples: He cracked a rib snowboarding.
You can count her ribs.
The dog got kicked in the ribs.

entries.meaning: The column of small bones running down the middle of the back. ---
examples: An injury to the spine can be permanent.
She has a slight curve in her spine.
He felt a chill run down his spine.

entries.meaning: A place where two bones meet and the body can bend. ---
examples: My joints ache when it rains.
The knee is the biggest joint in the body.
Arthritis inflames the joints.

entries.meaning: The hard covering on the end of a finger or toe. ---
examples: I broke a nail opening the box.
She bites her nails when she is nervous.
Keep your nails short for climbing.

entries.meaning: The hard covering on the end of a finger. ---
examples: He chewed his fingernails down to nothing.
There was dirt under her fingernails.
A fingernail takes about six months to grow out.

entries.meaning: The inner surface of the hand. ---
examples: She read the lines on my palm.
He pressed his palms together.
The coin was hidden in his palm.
entries.contrast: The l is silent: PAHM. Same word as the palm tree.

entries.meaning: A hand with the fingers curled tightly into the palm. ---
examples: He slammed his fist on the table.
The baby's tiny fists were clenched.
She kept the note crumpled in her fist.

entries.meaning: The part of the leg between the hip and the knee. ---
examples: He tore a muscle in his thigh.
The seat belt cut into my thighs.
Chicken thighs stay juicier than breasts.
entries.contrast: The -gh is silent: THY, rhyming with my.

entries.meaning: The front of the leg between the knee and the ankle. ---
examples: He kicked me in the shin.
I banged my shin on the bed frame.
Soccer players wear pads over their shins.

entries.meaning: The rounded back part of the foot. ---
examples: My heel blistered on the second day.
He turned on his heel and walked out.
These shoes rub my heels.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like heal.

entries.meaning: The underside of the foot. ---
examples: The soles of my feet were burning on the hot sand.
He has a splinter in the sole of his foot.
Walking barefoot toughens up your soles.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like soul.

entries.meaning: Either of the two fleshy parts of the body you sit on. ---
examples: He landed hard on one buttock.
The shot goes into the buttock.
She has a bruise across both buttocks.

entries.meaning: Either of the two soft round parts on the front of a woman's chest. ---
examples: She found a lump in her left breast.
Breast screening usually starts at forty.
The baby nursed at her breast.

entries.meaning: The small raised point in the middle of the breast. ---
examples: The baby would not latch onto the nipple.
She had a rash around one nipple.
The bottle came with two spare nipples.
entries.contrast: Americans call the rubber top of a baby bottle a nipple; British English says teat.

entries.meaning: The small hollow in the middle of the stomach. ---
examples: She has a piercing in her navel.
The scar runs just below the navel.
The doctor measured down from the navel.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like naval. In ordinary speech Americans say belly button.

entries.meaning: The part of the body between the chest and the hips, holding the digestive organs. ---
examples: The pain is low in the abdomen.
He was stabbed in the abdomen.
She felt a tightness across her abdomen.
entries.contrast: Americans usually stress the first syllable: AB-duh-mun.

entries.meaning: The trunk of the body, without the head, arms, or legs. ---
examples: The statue is just a torso, no head or arms.
He has tattoos across his whole torso.
The scan covered the torso only.

entries.meaning: An arm or a leg. ---
examples: The accident cost him a limb.
Surgeons reattached the severed limb.
Cold weather makes your limbs stiff.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: LIM.

entries.meaning: The soft tissue of the body between the skin and the bones. ---
examples: The blade cut into the flesh of his palm.
Mosquitoes went straight for any exposed flesh.
The bruise showed dark against pale flesh.

entries.meaning: The firm flexible tissue found in joints, the nose, and the ears. ---
examples: He tore the cartilage in his knee.
Your nose is mostly cartilage, not bone.
Cartilage heals slowly because it has no blood supply.

entries.meaning: A tough cord that attaches a muscle to a bone. ---
examples: He ruptured a tendon in his ankle.
You can feel the tendons on the back of your hand.
The tendon runs from the calf down to the heel.

entries.meaning: A band of tissue that holds two bones together at a joint. ---
examples: She tore a ligament in her knee.
Ligaments hold the joint in place.
A stretched ligament takes months to heal.

entries.meaning: The material that the parts of a body are made of. ---
examples: Scar tissue built up around the wound.
The burn destroyed the surrounding tissue.
The lab grows human tissue in a dish.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Uncountable for body material; countable for the paper kind — hand me a tissue.

entries.meaning: A part of the body with a particular job, such as the heart or the liver. ---
examples: The liver is the largest internal organ.
He is registered as an organ donor.
Alcohol damages several organs at once.

entries.meaning: An organ that produces a substance the body uses or releases. ---
examples: The glands in my neck are swollen.
The thyroid is a small gland at the base of the throat.
Sweat glands cover most of the body.

entries.meaning: The smallest living unit that bodies are built from. ---
examples: The body replaces old cells constantly.
A single cell divides into two.
Red blood cells carry oxygen.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sell.

entries.meaning: All the bones of a body taken together. ---
examples: A human skeleton has 206 bones.
They found a skeleton buried under the floor.
The museum has a dinosaur skeleton in the lobby.

entries.meaning: The flat area on either side of the forehead, beside the eye. ---
examples: She rubbed her temples to fight off the headache.
Gray hair started at his temples.
The blow landed on his temple.
entries.contrast: Spelled and pronounced exactly like the religious building; only context separates them.

entries.meaning: The skin on top of the head, where the hair grows. ---
examples: The cut on his scalp bled a lot.
That shampoo leaves my scalp itchy.
Sunburn on the scalp is easy to get.

entries.meaning: The hair that grows on a man's chin and cheeks. ---
examples: He grew a beard over the winter.
There was food in his beard.
She likes him better without the beard.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with weird, not with heard.

entries.meaning: The hair a man grows on his upper lip. ---
examples: He shaved off his mustache.
Milk left a mustache on the kid's lip.
The old photo shows him with a thick mustache.
entries.contrast: Americans write mustache, the British moustache. English keeps it singular where Russian усы is plural: he has a mustache.

entries.meaning: The whole round part of the eye inside the socket. ---
examples: The doctor shined a light on his eyeball.
Her eyeballs were bloodshot.
The pressure inside the eyeball was too high.

entries.meaning: The black opening in the middle of the eye that light passes through. ---
examples: The doctor checked whether his pupils were reacting.
Her pupils went huge in the dark room.
One pupil was larger than the other.
entries.contrast: Same word as pupil meaning a school student.

entries.meaning: The colored ring around the pupil of the eye. ---
examples: She has a ring of gold around each iris.
The iris opens and closes to control the light.
His irises are almost black.

entries.meaning: The thin piece of skin inside the ear that vibrates with sound. ---
examples: The blast ruptured his eardrum.
Loud music can damage your eardrums.
The doctor looked at my eardrum with a light.

entries.meaning: Either of the two openings at the bottom of the nose. ---
examples: One nostril is always more blocked than the other.
He flared his nostrils.
The spray goes into each nostril.

entries.meaning: The firm pink flesh around the base of the teeth. ---
examples: My gums bleed when I floss.
The dentist said my gums look healthy.
Cold water hurts his gums.
entries.contrast: The chewing kind of gum is uncountable: a piece of gum, never a gum.

entries.meaning: One of the wide flat teeth at the back of the mouth used for grinding. ---
examples: The dentist pulled a molar.
He cracked a molar on a popcorn kernel.
Molars do most of the chewing.

entries.meaning: Either of the two small masses of tissue at the back of the throat. ---
examples: They took out her tonsils when she was six.
His tonsils are swollen again.
The infection settled in one tonsil.

entries.meaning: The tube that carries air from the throat down to the lungs. ---
examples: A piece of food went down his windpipe.
The smoke burned her windpipe.
The surgeon opened the windpipe so he could breathe.

entries.meaning: The long tube below the stomach where food is digested and absorbed. ---
examples: The infection was in his small intestine.
The large intestine absorbs water.
Human intestines are surprisingly long.

entries.meaning: The intestine, especially the lower part of it. ---
examples: He has trouble with his bowels.
The surgeon removed part of the bowel.
Bowel problems run in the family.

entries.meaning: The stomach and intestines, in informal speech. ---
examples: He took a punch in the gut.
The fish was cleaned and its guts thrown out.
Bacteria in the gut help you digest food.

entries.meaning: The organ that holds urine before it leaves the body. ---
examples: Coffee irritates my bladder.
The infection was in her bladder.
He has a small bladder and stops at every rest area.

entries.meaning: The organ near the stomach that filters blood and fights infection. ---
examples: The accident ruptured his spleen.
Surgeons had to remove her spleen.
The spleen clears out old blood cells.

entries.meaning: The gland behind the stomach that makes insulin and digestive juices. ---
examples: The pancreas makes insulin.
Heavy drinking can inflame the pancreas.
They found a tumor on his pancreas.

entries.meaning: The small organ under the liver that stores bile. ---
examples: They took out my gallbladder last year.
Fatty food set off her gallbladder.
The gallbladder stores bile until you eat.

entries.meaning: The organ in a woman's body where a baby grows. ---
examples: The baby moved in her womb.
Twins share a womb for nine months.
The scan showed the womb was healthy.
entries.contrast: The b is silent and the o says oo: WOOM.

entries.meaning: Either of the two organs in a woman's body that produce eggs. ---
examples: The cyst was on her left ovary.
The ovaries release one egg a month.
The surgeon removed both ovaries.

entries.meaning: The clear liquid produced in the mouth. ---
examples: The smell filled my mouth with saliva.
The test uses a saliva sample.
Saliva starts breaking food down before you swallow.

entries.meaning: The salty liquid the skin gives off when the body is hot. ---
examples: Sweat was running into my eyes.
His shirt was soaked with sweat.
Sweat cools you down as it evaporates.

entries.meaning: A drop of the liquid that comes from the eye when you cry. ---
examples: A tear ran down her cheek.
He wiped away a tear.
The onions had all of us in tears.
entries.contrast: This tear rhymes with here; the unrelated verb tear, meaning rip, rhymes with air.

entries.meaning: One movement of air into or out of the lungs. ---
examples: Take a deep breath.
He was out of breath after one flight of stairs.
She held her breath underwater.
entries.contrast: The noun breath has a short e and a voiceless th; the verb breathe has a long ee and a voiced th.

entries.meaning: The regular beat of blood that you can feel in an artery. ---
examples: The nurse took my pulse.
His pulse was weak but steady.
She could feel her pulse in her ears.

entries.meaning: A joint in the finger, especially where the finger meets the hand. ---
examples: He cracked his knuckles.
Her knuckles were white on the steering wheel.
He skinned a knuckle on the engine block.
entries.contrast: The k is silent: NUK-ul.

entries.meaning: The hollow under the arm where it joins the body. ---
examples: Deodorant goes under the armpit.
He had a rash in his armpit.
Her shirt was soaked at the armpits.

entries.meaning: Either of the two bones running from the shoulder to the base of the neck. ---
examples: He broke his collarbone in the crash.
You can see her collarbones in that dress.
The strap dug into my collarbone.

entries.meaning: The small round bone at the front of the knee. ---
examples: The surgeon replaced his kneecap.
She landed on her kneecaps.
A blow to the kneecap is agony.

entries.meaning: The thick bundle of nerves running down inside the spine. ---
examples: The injury damaged his spinal cord.
The spinal cord carries signals from the brain to the body.
Nerves branch off the spinal cord all the way down.
entries.contrast: Cord, not chord — the two sound identical but only cord is the body part.

entries.meaning: The soft tissue inside bones where blood cells are made. ---
examples: He needs a bone marrow transplant.
Marrow makes new blood cells every day.
The doctors tested her marrow for cancer.

entries.meaning: One of the tiny openings in the skin that sweat comes out of. ---
examples: Hot water opens your pores.
That cream clogged my pores.
Sweat comes out through the pores.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like pour.

entries.meaning: A small line in the skin that comes with age. ---
examples: She has fine wrinkles around her eyes.
The cream promises to smooth out wrinkles.
A deep wrinkle ran across his forehead.
entries.contrast: The w is silent: RING-kul.

entries.meaning: A small light brown spot on the skin, usually from the sun. ---
examples: He has freckles across his nose.
Summer brings out her freckles.
A single freckle sat on her cheek.

entries.meaning: A small hollow in the cheek or chin that shows when someone smiles. ---
examples: She has a dimple in one cheek.
His dimples show when he smiles.
The baby has a dimple on her chin.

entries.meaning: A small dark permanent spot on the skin. ---
examples: The doctor removed a mole from his back.
She has a small mole above her lip.
Watch any mole that changes shape or color.
entries.contrast: Same word as the burrowing animal.

entries.meaning: The natural color and condition of the skin on someone's face. ---
examples: She has a fair complexion.
The medication cleared up his complexion.
Sleep does more for your complexion than any cream.

entries.meaning: The end of a finger, past the last joint. ---
examples: He touched the screen with one fingertip.
Her fingertips were numb from the cold.
There are nerve endings all over your fingertips.

entries.meaning: The part of the arm between the elbow and the wrist. ---
examples: He has a tattoo on his left forearm.
She blocked the ball with her forearm.
His forearms got huge from climbing.

entries.meaning: The flat surface formed by the upper legs when a person is sitting. ---
examples: The cat fell asleep in my lap.
She held the baby on her lap.
He balanced the plate on his lap.
entries.contrast: Russian на коленях is the English lap, not knees — a child sits on your lap.

entries.meaning: The area where the legs meet the front of the body. ---
examples: He pulled a muscle in his groin.
The pain started in his groin.
Groin injuries end a lot of seasons early.

entries.meaning: The ring of bone at the base of the spine that the legs attach to. ---
examples: The X-ray showed a fractured pelvis.
The baby's head has to pass through the pelvis.
She landed on her pelvis and couldn't get up.

entries.meaning: One of the hollow spaces in the bones around the nose. ---
examples: My sinuses are killing me today.
The infection spread to his sinuses.
Cold air clears out my sinuses.

entries.meaning: The main part of the large intestine. ---
examples: He is scheduled for a colon screening.
The surgeon removed part of the colon.
Fiber keeps the colon working.
entries.contrast: Same word as the punctuation mark.

entries.meaning: The sheet of muscle below the lungs that moves when you breathe. ---
examples: Singers learn to breathe from the diaphragm.
The diaphragm pulls air into the lungs.
A spasm in the diaphragm is what causes hiccups.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: DY-uh-fram.

entries.meaning: The soft tissue under the skin that stores energy. ---
examples: Running burns fat slowly.
He has lost a lot of body fat this year.
Fat under the skin helps keep you warm.

entries.meaning: The soft hanging part at the bottom of the ear. ---
examples: She has three piercings in one earlobe.
He tugged at his earlobe while he thought.
My earlobes were bright red from the cold.

entries.meaning: Either of the two bones just below the eyes. ---
examples: She has high cheekbones.
The punch broke his cheekbone.
Shadows fell under his cheekbones.

entries.meaning: One of the tendons or muscles at the back of the thigh.
examples: He pulled a hamstring in the first quarter.
Hamstring injuries take weeks to heal.
Stretch your hamstrings before you run.
